title: Indian Banks Face a Q2 Paradox: FCNR Flood Boosts Loans, Squeezes Margins
excerpt: Brokerages expect Q2FY27 bank earnings to rise about 11%, powered by 18.8% credit growth and $127 billion of FCNR deposits — but the foreign-currency funding is set to shave 8–20 basis points off net interest margins.
body:
• Kotak Institutional Equities expects Indian banks to report roughly 11% year-on-year earnings growth in Q2FY27, with net interest income also rising about 11%; private banks are forecast to grow earnings around 20%, while public-sector lenders stay broadly flat.
  • Banks mobilised about $127 billion through FCNR(B) deposits under the RBI's swap window between June 8 and August 31, 2026 — roughly 4.5% of system deposits — pushing system deposit growth to around 17% year-on-year from 11–12%.
  • The foreign-currency flood is a double-edged sword: systemic credit growth reached 18.8% year-on-year by September 15, but analysts expect net interest margins to compress 8–20 basis points this quarter, as costly FCNR funds sit partly undeployed in lower-yielding investments.
  • For NRI depositors: FCNR(B) deposits carry no currency risk — the bank absorbs rupee fluctuations — but with banks now flush with liquidity, deposit rates are likely to soften in the second half of FY27; anyone parking fresh NRI money may get better terms locking in current rates now.

Indian banks enter the September-quarter results season with a paradox: a flood of foreign-currency deposits from non-resident Indians has supercharged lending capacity but is set to squeeze the margins that drive profits. Kotak Institutional Equities expects the sector to report roughly 11% year-on-year earnings growth in Q2FY27 — solid, yet weighed down by the cost of the very deposits powering that growth.

Context & Background

Between June 8 and August 31, 2026, Indian banks raised about $127 billion through Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) — FCNR(B) — deposits under a Reserve Bank of India swap window, equivalent to about 4.5% of the banking system's deposit base as of March 31, 2026, according to S&P Global Ratings. FCNR(B) accounts let NRIs hold deposits in foreign currency — dollars, pounds, euros — with the bank absorbing all exchange-rate risk.

The inflows transformed the funding picture. Motilal Oswal Financial Services estimates system deposit growth accelerated to about 17% year-on-year from 11–12% previously, and the system-wide credit-deposit ratio eased to 80.8% from a peak of 83.4%. Systemic credit growth hit 18.8% year-on-year as of September 15, 2026, driven by retail borrowing, higher utilisation among micro, small and medium enterprises, and healthy corporate demand.

Impact & Analysis

The catch: FCNR money is expensive. The deposits cost more than low-cost current and savings account (CASA) funds, and a large share has not yet been deployed as loans — it sits in lower-yielding investments and short-term placements. Kotak estimates banks with large FCNR books could see net interest margins decline 10–20 basis points in the September quarter. Motilal Oswal puts private-bank margin compression at 8–20 basis points.

Business updates from 21 banks underline the scale. Aggregate deposits rose 15.3% year-on-year to ₹173.5 lakh crore in the September quarter, while advances grew faster at 21.4% year-on-year to ₹149.6 lakh crore — pushing the group's credit-deposit ratio to 86.3% from 82% a year earlier. Kotak Mahindra Bank was the standout, with deposits up 13.7% sequentially; HDFC Bank grew deposits 19%, outpacing its loan growth of over 15%, and cut its credit-deposit ratio to 95.7% from 98.8%.

The pain looks temporary. Kotak expects the drag to fade in the second half of FY27 as banks deploy the liquidity into loans and replace expensive wholesale funding. Private banks are forecast to lead the quarter: net profit up 24% year-on-year, net interest income up 13%, with ICICI Bank's NII seen growing 16.8%, followed by Kotak Mahindra at 14%, HDFC Bank at 8.9% and Axis Bank at 8.5%, according to Motilal Oswal.

"Future growth of such deposits is unlikely to recur at this scale. Banks could face refinancing and repricing pressure, if they make up a sizable portion of overall deposits."

— Geeta Chugh, Credit Analyst, S&P Global Ratings

Diaspora Angle

For the NRI depositors who supplied this $127 billion, the mechanics are reassuring: FCNR(B) deposits are denominated in foreign currency, so a depositor's returns are untouched by rupee swings — the bank takes the currency risk. But the same flood that made these deposits attractive to banks could make them less rewarding going forward. As funding costs ease in the second half of FY27, banks typically trim the rates they offer on fresh NRI deposits. NRIs considering new FCNR(B) placements — or rolling over maturing ones — may find today's rates are the high-water mark for this cycle.

What's Next

The September-quarter results, due through October, will show how much margin pain materialised and how fast banks are converting FCNR liquidity into loans. The longer test comes in 2029–2031, when the three-to-five-year FCNR deposits begin maturing in bunches: banks with strong franchises should refinance smoothly, S&P says, but weaker ones could face a squeeze. For investors, the quarter's real question is not whether lending grows — it is whether banks can deploy the money at yields that justify its cost.
